stories.headline: Cursor adds Z.ai's GLM 5.3 and says it tops open models
stories.standfirst: Cursor says GLM 5.3 Max is the best-scoring open-weight model on its own CursorBench 4.0, and has added both GLM 5.3 and a Flash variant to its editor.
body: Cursor said on X on Thursday evening that GLM 5.3 and GLM 5.3 Flash are now available in its coding editor. In the same post the company said GLM 5.3 Max is the best-scoring open-weight model on CursorBench 4.0, a benchmark Cursor runs itself. The post had about 900 likes when we read it.

The scoring claim is Cursor's alone. We have not seen the CursorBench 4.0 methodology or the scores, and no outside group has published a comparison. Cursor's post does not say what a Max tier is or how it differs from the base model. Z.ai, the Chinese lab behind GLM, had not commented in the material we reviewed.

GLM-5.3 itself dates from August. According to an NYU Shanghai research note, Z.ai announced it on 14 August as a 743-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model on the same base as June's GLM-5.2, with every gain coming from longer post-training. Z.ai held the weights back for roughly two weeks for a safety review.

The NYU note reports Z.ai's own coding numbers: Terminal-Bench rose from 4.6 to 28.3 and DeepSWE from 46.2 to 66.9 against GLM-5.2. It also says the model found 2,436 vulnerabilities across 269 open-source projects, 1,097 of them rated critical or high. Those figures come from Z.ai and have not been independently checked.

Gigazine reported that the weights went public on 29 August under a bespoke GLM-5.3 licence that requires a Z.ai security review for companies with more than $10 billion in annual revenue. The licence terms matter for anyone planning to ship the model inside a product, and they should be read directly.

stories.headline: Judge dismisses Chegg and Penske suits over Google's AI Overviews
stories.standfirst: US District Judge Amit Mehta wrote that publishers' "expectation" of search traffic "is not an agreement", throwing out two antitrust suits over Google's AI-written search summaries.
body: A federal judge has dismissed antitrust lawsuits that Chegg and Penske Media, the parent company of Rolling Stone, brought against Google over its AI Overviews search feature, according to The Verge, Engadget and Ars Technica. US District Judge Amit Mehta ruled for Google on Wednesday, The Verge reported.

The suits accused Google of driving readers away from publishers' sites with AI-powered search features, The Verge reported. Engadget described two claims. Google allegedly used AI Overviews to divert readers and revenue by repackaging content. It also allegedly forced sites to supply content for AI use or risk exclusion from search.

Mehta found that neither company showed Google had broken antitrust law or used a search monopoly as leverage, Engadget reported. The outlet quoted his ruling: "Plaintiffs have pleaded only that they have an 'expectation' that Google will send them search traffic if they make their content available for free. But an expectation is not an agreement."

Ars Technica summarised the ruling as acknowledging that AI search has consequences without treating them as an antitrust matter. Engadget noted that Mehta found in 2024 that Google maintained a search monopoly. Its report did not say whether the dismissals are with or without prejudice, or whether either company will appeal.

Engadget said it had asked Penske Media and Chegg for comment and had not heard back at publication. Its report carried no statement from Google. Engadget also noted that publishers can exclude content from AI Overviews while remaining in ordinary search results, though AI features increasingly dominate results pages.

stories.headline: CBS reports Jay Clayton is likely Trump's pick for AI czar
stories.standfirst: CBS News, citing sources, says Jay Clayton will likely be named the White House's AI czar while staying director of national intelligence. The White House calls the reporting baseless speculation.
body: CBS News reported on Thursday, citing multiple sources briefed on the matter, that Jay Clayton is likely to be President Trump's choice as the White House's AI czar. The sources said Clayton may keep his current job as director of national intelligence while taking the new role, which would put one official over both the intelligence agencies and AI policy.

The report is not confirmed. A White House official told CBS that any personnel announcement would come directly from the President, and that any reporting before then was baseless speculation. CBS described its story as breaking and subject to updates, and we have not seen a second outlet confirm the choice.

The post has been vacant on paper since Trump said last month that he would appoint an AI czar. According to CBS, he described the role then with the line "Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!", and the choice has since been the subject of speculation in Washington.

CBS says the timing follows a White House meeting at which leaders of major AI companies signed voluntary safety standards. After it, the outlet reports, Trump told reporters he planned to name someone within three or four days and called the candidate "extraordinary". That window has now passed without an announcement, as far as CBS reports.

What the job would cover is not defined in the CBS report, including whether it would carry authority over agencies or act as an adviser. Those details, and whether Clayton would hold both posts at once, would only be settled by an official announcement, which the White House has not made.

stories.headline: Satlyt raises $8 million to run AI models on other companies' satellites
stories.standfirst: Satlyt says it has already run Google DeepMind's Gemma model on a Momentus spacecraft, cutting the size of error reports sent to the ground by more than 60%.
body: Satlyt, a startup that writes software for running AI models on satellites, has raised an $8 million seed round led by Houston-based Non Sibi Ventures, TechCrunch reported on Thursday. The company does not build satellites. Chief executive Rama Afullo told TechCrunch it aims to be a software layer that works across many operators' spacecraft.

Afullo previously worked in Google's cloud division and briefly at SpaceX's Starlink, and pitched orbital computing inside both before founding Satlyt, with offices in Sunnyvale and Nairobi, according to TechCrunch. He contrasted the company's open approach with what the outlet called SpaceX's closed, all-in-one, iPhone-style model.

The company says it has completed two demonstration missions. In one it deployed Google DeepMind's Gemma model on a Momentus spacecraft, which TechCrunch says cut the size of software error reports sent to the ground by more than 60%. A third mission is due to launch this week on a TakeMe2Space satellite, with NASA and Stellerian among its customers.

Afullo told TechCrunch he wants Satlyt on 20% of satellites by 2030, and expects builders to treat a processor as standard kit. "You're putting up a satellite without putting up a GPU on it, at the very least, you're doing yourself a disservice," he said. The 20% figure is the founder's goal, not a forecast we can check.

Big companies are testing the same idea. International Cyber Digest reported on Thursday that Google launched one of its AI chips into orbit for the first time, on a Planet Labs-built satellite carried by a SpaceX rocket, as the first hardware test for Project Suncatcher. It said Google estimates space data centres need about 1,800 Starship flights over ten years, a figure we have not verified.

stories.headline: OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra Ultrafast generates tokens up to 8x faster, Nvidia says
stories.standfirst: Nvidia says a new Ultrafast mode of GPT-6 Astra, running on Blackwell GPUs, produces tokens up to eight times faster than Astra Standard and is live in the API.
body: Nvidia said on Thursday that GPT-6 Astra Ultrafast, a faster serving mode of OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra, is available now in the OpenAI API and to eligible ChatGPT Work and Codex users. The company says it offers up to eight times faster token generation than Astra Standard, and runs on Nvidia Blackwell GPUs.

The speed figure comes from Nvidia's own blog post, which describes the mode as aimed at coding, tool use and interactive applications. It gives no benchmark method, no baseline hardware and no latency numbers, and the phrase up to means typical gains may be lower. OpenAI's own announcement was not part of the material we reviewed.

The post does not state a price, and sends readers to an Ultrafast guide for it. Faster serving modes usually cost more per token, but the size of any premium here is not confirmed. Developers should check the guide before moving production traffic onto the new mode.

Nvidia quotes two OpenAI executives. Philippe Tillet, its inference lead, said Nvidia's tooling and documentation helped OpenAI make its models exceptionally good at programming Blackwell. Uday Ruddarraju, its chief technology officer of compute, said OpenAI used internal models to optimise inference on Nvidia GPUs, and that this allows continuing gains after launch.

stories.headline: TestingCatalog reports Black Forest Labs' FLUX 3 Image is live in a playground
stories.standfirst: TestingCatalog says Black Forest Labs has announced FLUX 3 Image with 4K output and precise editing, with open weights planned for the coming weeks.
body: TestingCatalog, a site that reports on features found in apps and live tests, said late on Thursday that Black Forest Labs has announced FLUX 3 Image, a new image model for precise editing with support for 4K output. Users can already try the new features in the company's Tools Playground, it said, and open weights are planned within weeks.

This is a single-outlet report and the company's own page for the release was not available to us. TestingCatalog's post carries a video of the features. We could not confirm the 4K claim, the availability or the timing of open weights from Black Forest Labs, and the findings stay unconfirmed until the company confirms them.

The model was flagged earlier. Black Forest Labs' FLUX 3 announcement, dated 23 July, said FLUX 3 can synthesise and edit images in a wide range of styles, aspect ratios and resolutions. It said an early-access phase for FLUX 3 Image would open in the following weeks, and that open weights would come as FLUX 3 Dev over weeks and months.

That earlier post named no price or date for the image tier. If TestingCatalog is right, the playground release would be the first time the image model has been in public hands. The open-weights release matters most to the local-image community, which has built on earlier FLUX checkpoints, though no licence terms have been published.
